# Leadership Strategies That Build Stronger Teams


Published: 11/17/2026


Table of Contents


- What Sets a Leadership Strategy Apart From a Style, Trait, or Behavior
- 4 Leadership Strategies That Build Stronger Teams
- How to Implement High-Trust Leadership Strategies During Disruption
- Strengthen Team Performance Through a Connected Leadership Strategy


Recent FranklinCovey research shows that[two out of three employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) report low confidence in the quality of today’s leaders. That gap often shows up when leaders lack a consistent way of turning their vision into the daily decisions and actions that move a team forward—in other words, when they don’t have a clear leadership strategy.


**So, what are leadership strategies?** They are deliberate systems a leader builds to achieve a specific outcome, made up of several coordinated behaviors. A well-defined leadership strategy gives leaders a clearer framework for deciding where to focus their time and how to support their teams.


The strategies below are organized around outcomes and results, drawing on FranklinCovey’s proven frameworks for execution and team leadership.


### Key Takeaways:


- A leadership strategy is a coordinated system of behaviors designed to accomplish a specific outcome.
- When leadership strategies fail, it’s typically because the underlying behaviors are not connected into one deliberate system.
- Leaders build stronger teams by committing to one or two strong strategies at a time rather than adding isolated habits one at a time.


## What Sets a Leadership Strategy Apart From a Style, Trait, or Behavior


## Management works in the system; leadership works on the system.


— Stephen R. Covey


These terms are often used interchangeably, but they actually describe different things:


- A **leadership trait** is internal and largely unobservable, such as confidence or empathy.
- A **leadership style** is a general pattern a leader leans toward, such as transformational or situational leadership.
- A **leadership behavior** is a single or repeatable observable action in a moment, such as asking a question or delivering feedback.
- A **leadership strategy** is the deliberate system that connects several behaviors to a specific outcome, such as stronger execution, faster decisions, or a more resilient team.


A single behavior can **support** a strategy, but it would not be described as a strategy on its own. For example,[seeking first to understand](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/the-7-habits/habit-5/) someone else’s perspective before responding is a great habit on its own; it can also be used to support a larger leadership strategy. A leader who commits to a consistent communication strategy builds something a team can rely on because the habit is tied to a deliberate outcome and reinforced consistently.

## 4 Leadership Strategies That Build Stronger Teams


Each strategy below brings together specific behaviors into a system designed to support a clear outcome. Grounded in proven FranklinCovey principles, these strategies can be put into practice right away to start strengthening leadership.


### 1. Focus Priorities and Track Progress


Despite significant investment, most strategies fail. But the failure point is rarely the strategy itself. Instead, it’s what happens (or doesn’t happen) once the decision is made.


This leadership strategy has two parts: narrow to a small number of Wildly Important Goals® instead of a long list of priorities, then track the specific actions that predict progress toward them rather than waiting to review the final result.


Only about[half of employees strongly agree](https://news.gallup.com/businessjournal/195803/employees-really-know-expected.aspx) that they know what is expected of them at work. That lack of clarity makes it difficult for teams to translate broader strategies into defined priorities and actions. Communication, delegation, and development all work better once a team has clearly determined its priorities.


**Download our guide,**[8 Ways to Boost Your Team’s Commitment to Goals](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-8-ways-to-boost?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) **, to create clarity, refine your top priorities, and inspire accountability for outcomes.**


### 2. Give Teams Decision-Making Autonomy


A team’s ability to move forward depends on how quickly it can make decisions. FranklinCovey research finds that[more than a third of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-ai-transformation-human-imperative?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) hesitate to make decisions without their manager’s approval, which slows a team down even when everyone already agrees on the plan.


This leadership strategy requires determining who is closest to the work and ready to own the decisions, then deliberately[handing decisions off](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/6-critical-practices/delegate-to-elevate/) instead of routing everything through one person by default. Handing off a decision also signals trust; teams only move at full speed once that trust is established.


The payoff is measurable: Research shows CEOs with strong delegation skills generate[33% more revenue](https://news.gallup.com/businessjournal/182414/delegating-huge-management-challenge-entrepreneurs.aspx) than those with weak delegation skills. However, the strategy may fail if a leader pulls decision-making authority back the moment something goes wrong. Leaders need to reassess and coach readiness rather than treat a setback as a reason to reclaim the decision permanently, since pulling authority back erodes the same trust the strategy depends on.


### 3. Build a Consistent Rhythm of 1-on-1s and Feedback


Leaders who hold a 1-on-1 meetings consistently give their teams an established channel for the kind of feedback that drives engagement. Data shows[80% of employees](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/505370/great-manager-important-habit.aspx) who received meaningful feedback in the past week report being fully engaged, and employees who receive feedback weekly or more often show a[48% engagement rate](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/651812/organizations-redefine-feedback-including-recognition.aspx) , compared to just 5% for employees who receive feedback annually or less.


This strategy requires setting a specific cadence, with a standing weekly or biweekly 1-on-1 that is rarely cancelled, paired with feedback that explains what happened, what was done well, and what to do differently going forward.


**Download our guide,**[100+ Questions for Better 1-on-1s With Your Direct Reports](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-100-questions-for-better-1-on-1s?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) **, to drive engagement, commitment, and performance *.***


### 4. Communicate Decisions With Context


Research reveals[87% of business leaders](https://www.grammarly.com/business/Grammarly_The_State_Of_Business_Communication.pdf) agree their teams cannot meet their goals without effective communication skills, and yet, many leaders simply state what was decided without explaining why.


Good[communication skills](https://www.franklincovey.com/why-franklincovey/leadership/communication-and-collaboration/) give teams the context they need to act on a decision. Leaders need to consistently explain the reasoning behind it and adjust the level of detail based on what each person needs to know. When teams understand why a decision was made, they’re better equipped to handle similar decisions on their own instead of bringing every question back to the leader. They’re also more likely to remain committed to their goals, their team, and their organization if leaders are transparent about the “why” and not just the “what.”


Space for questions matters, too. When leaders give people a chance to clarify what they don’t understand and raise concerns or perspectives the leader may have missed, they’ll help their team understand the decision, their role in the work, and what it means for their day-to-day life.

## How to Implement High-Trust Leadership Strategies During Disruption


## People are working harder than ever, but because they lack clarity and vision, they aren’t getting very far. They, in essence, are pushing a rope with all of their might.


— Stephen R. Covey


According to Gartner,[79% of employees](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-07-08-gartner-hr-research-finds-just-32-percent-of-business-leaders-report-achieving-healthy-change-adoption-by-employees) report low trust during change. What’s more, just[42% of employees surveyed by FranklinCovey](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) view their own leaders as trusted. When workplace trust is already low, adding new strategies can feel like another confusing disruption rather than a meaningful improvement.


Here are some steps leaders can take to build trust and engagement during periods of disruption and uncertainty:


- Start with the strategy that addresses the biggest gap on your team, and give people time to make it part of their routine before adding something new.[Leading through change](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/change-leadership/) requires patience, and teams are more likely to stick with one new habit than with several changes introduced at once.
- Recognize where your people currently sit on the[change curve](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/change/) . While every change is unique, it always follows a predictable pattern. Once you know where someone is, you can help them navigate to the next stage.
- Watch for signs that a strategy isn’t sticking. Missed follow-through or a return to old habits may mean the team needs more support or reinforcement.
- Ask the team how the change is going. People experiencing the strategy firsthand may notice confusion or challenges that aren’t visible from the leader’s perspective.

## Strengthen Team Performance With a Connected Leadership Strategy


Leadership strategies become more effective as leaders adjust them to meet team needs and priorities. When those practices are carefully maintained, teams can make decisions with less oversight, recover from setbacks more independently, and take on greater responsibility.


Turning leadership strategies into lasting impact takes consistency and follow-through.
